ecb-2026-09.standing: The European Central Bank's Governing Council, which sets the single policy rate for the twenty countries sharing the euro. It meets eight times a year, and its decisions set the cost of borrowing for roughly 350 million people across economies with very different exposures.
ecb-2026-09.recent: Deutsche Bank has raised where it expects the ECB's tightening to end, to 2.75%, on the argument that an energy shock is feeding into second-round wage and price effects rather than passing through once. That is the split in front of the Council: whether an import-driven price rise is something to look through or something already lodged in domestic costs. What the meeting settles is how much further the euro area's borrowers are asked to absorb.

fomc-2026-09.standing: The Federal Open Market Committee, the twelve-member body that sets the US federal funds rate eight times a year. It is the reference price for dollar credit worldwide, and borrowing costs from mortgages to emerging-market debt reprice off it.
fomc-2026-09.recent: Warsh arrives at this meeting having spent Jackson Hole arguing the case for tightening, and a payroll surge since has pushed hike odds to two-in-three. The committee is weighing an oil shock feeding imported inflation against a 30-year mortgage rate at 6.71% that is already squeezing US borrowers, and what it settles is whether the Fed treats the supply shock as something to lean against.

boe-2026-09.standing: The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee, which meets eight times a year to set Bank Rate. Its votes are published individually, and the rate flows into British mortgages, business lending and the pound.
boe-2026-09.recent: Governor Andrew Bailey has spent the run-up warning the G20 that AI models pose new risks to financial stability, an argument about the system the Bank supervises rather than the rate it sets. The committee meets into a global bond selloff that has pushed yields to multi-decade highs on inflation fears — a long end the MPC does not control, while the part it does decides what British borrowers pay.

boj-2026-09.standing: Japan's central bank, whose policy board meets eight times a year to set the short-term policy rate and steer government bond purchases. It is the last major central bank to have left negative rates behind, and the yen carries its decisions into global funding markets.
boj-2026-09.recent: The board meets after the yen fell past 160 per dollar, a level that has drawn intervention before and that widens the gap between Japanese rates and everyone else's. The Bank of Korea has already hiked to 3.00% citing financial stability, and markets have moved toward a September hike in Washington — leaving Tokyo deciding how much of the currency's slide is its own to answer for.

uk-cpi-2026-10.standing: The UK's monthly inflation reading from the Office for National Statistics, covering a basket of household goods and services. It sets the reference for the Bank of England's 2% target, index-linked gilts, and the annual uprating of pensions and benefits.

fomc-2026-10.standing: The rate-setting committee of the US central bank, which meets eight times a year to set the federal funds rate. It is the price of overnight dollar credit, and because the dollar is the world's funding currency, borrowing costs far outside America move with it.
fomc-2026-10.recent: Warsh arrives at this decision having spent his Jackson Hole debut repricing the dollar rather than settling the question. A payroll surge pushed hike odds to two-in-three, and the committee now has to say whether an oil shock is a supply move it looks through or an inflation it answers — a question the 30-year mortgage rate at 6.71% has already made concrete for US borrowers.

ecb-2026-10.standing: The European Central Bank's Governing Council, which sets the policy rate for the twenty countries that share the euro. Its decisions set borrowing costs for some 350 million people, and the euro curve prices debt far beyond the bloc.

boj-2026-10.standing: Japan's central bank, whose policy board sets the short-term rate and the pace of its bond purchases at eight scheduled meetings a year. It is the last of the major monetary authorities to keep rates near zero, and the yen carries the difference.
boj-2026-10.recent: The yen fell past 160 per dollar in Tokyo before this meeting, a level that has drawn intervention in the past and that the board cannot address without narrowing the rate gap it has held open. Markets now favor a September hike in Washington, which would widen that gap further, and the Bank of Korea has already hiked to 3.00%.

boe-2026-11.standing: The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee, nine members who vote individually on Bank Rate at eight scheduled meetings a year. The rate feeds through to British mortgages, business lending and the pound, and each vote split is published.
boe-2026-11.recent: Governor Andrew Bailey has spent the run-up warning the G20 that AI models pose new risks to financial stability, an argument about the system the Bank supervises rather than the rate it sets. The decision itself lands into a global bond selloff that has driven yields to multi-decade highs on inflation fears, and settles how far British borrowing costs follow.

fomc-2026-12.standing: The Federal Open Market Committee, which sets the US federal funds rate at eight scheduled meetings a year. The rate it picks is the anchor for dollar borrowing costs worldwide, feeding through to mortgages, corporate credit and emerging-market debt.
fomc-2026-12.recent: The committee arrives at this meeting after a payroll surge pushed hike odds to two-in-three, an oil shock that argues for tightening rather than easing, and a long-end selloff that took the 10-year Treasury yield to 4.81% and the 30-year mortgage rate to 6.71% without any policy move behind it. Warsh's Jackson Hole debut repriced the dollar; this decision settles whether that signal was policy.

g20-2026-miami.standing: The annual meeting of heads of state and government from nineteen countries, the European Union and the African Union, together roughly four-fifths of world output. It has no treaty powers; its product is a consensus communiqué every member must sign.
g20-2026-miami.recent: The US presidency has spent the year splitting the room it will chair: Treasury has been pressing other members to join its case against China's surplus, while European finance ministers boycotted the family photo over Siluanov's return to the table. Andrew Bailey used the finance track to warn the group that AI could trigger a global downturn. A summit whose only output is unanimous language now has to find some.

ecb-2026-12.standing: The euro area's rate-setting body, whose Governing Council meets roughly every six weeks to set the deposit rate that anchors borrowing costs across twenty member states. Its decisions price credit for some 350 million people.
ecb-2026-12.recent: Deutsche Bank has raised its expected ECB peak to 2.75%, arguing that energy risk is feeding through to second-round wage and services pricing rather than fading as a one-off. That is the argument in front of the Council in December: whether a supply shock it has no instrument to reach justifies squeezing the rest of the basket, with euro-priced borrowers from Cairo to Ankara paying the refinancing cost of a decision made in Frankfurt.

boe-2026-12.standing: The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee, whose nine members vote individually eight times a year on Bank Rate. That rate sets what British savers earn and what tracker and newly fixed mortgages cost across the UK.
boe-2026-12.recent: Andrew Bailey has spent the weeks before this meeting warning about something else: he told the G20 that AI poses a downturn risk to the global economy, and that AI models bring new dangers to financial stability. The December vote is where the committee's reading of those risks has to become a number.

boj-2026-12.standing: Japan's central bank, whose policy board meets eight times a year to set the short-term policy rate and steer the government bond market. It is the world's largest creditor nation's rate-setter, and the yen and global carry trades move with it.
boj-2026-12.recent: The yen fell past 160 per dollar in August, the level that has drawn intervention before, and the gap between Japanese and US rates is what is driving it — with markets now favoring a September Federal Reserve hike, that gap widens before the board even sits. The Bank of Korea has already hiked to 3.00%; this decision settles whether Tokyo follows or lets the currency carry the adjustment.

fred-us-ppi-2026-09-10.standing: The Bureau of Labor Statistics' monthly measure of what US producers receive for their output — the price of goods and services before they reach a shop shelf. It runs a month ahead of consumer inflation and feeds directly into the Fed's preferred price gauge.

fred-us-cpi-2026-09-11.standing: The monthly consumer price index from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, a survey of what households actually pay across housing, food, energy and services. It is the single number that anchors Federal Reserve policy and reprices debt worldwide.
fred-us-cpi-2026-09-11.recent: This release lands with the argument over the Fed already inverted: a payroll surge and an oil shock pushed hike odds to two-in-three, and Warsh is weighing imported inflation running through the dollar rather than the slowdown a cut would answer. The print settles whether the price pressure is energy passing through or something broader.

fred-us-retail-sales-2026-09-16.standing: The Census Bureau's monthly tally of receipts at US retail and food-service businesses, published about two weeks after the month it covers. Consumer spending drives most of the American economy, so the print moves rate expectations.
